4857-history-of-the-united-netherlands-1:
Philip II at his writing desk is the unlikely center of this 1588 volume, and John Lothrop Motley watches the Armada take shape from the Escorial. The king works through a handful of secretaries, nurses vast and vague schemes of conquest, and sends a fleet whose junction with Parma was never properly arranged.

A gale off Finisterre scatters the ships, David Gwynn performs his exploit, and the first Channel engagements cost Spain dearly. Near Portland the English show superior seamanship in a general engagement. Motley pairs court paperwork with sea battle, showing how a grand design failed in the details of wind, supply, and command.
history-of-the-united-netherlands-1588c:
John Lothrop Motley pauses his History of the United Netherlands in chapter nineteen to portrait Philip II in his cabinet. The king's system of work and deception governs empires from a desk. Spain and Italy wrote beautifully in that day, Motley notes. Philip's scrawl was like that of a clown just admitted to a writing school.

Across fifty-page despatches the royal margin carried a few awkward sentences, almost impossible to read. When deciphered, they revealed suggestions of astounding triviality. The most powerful man alive ruled by annotation, delay, and distrust of every servant. This famous character study explains the war's strange tempo: campaigns waited on one man's pen. Motley makes bureaucracy itself a tragic force, as fleets sail late because a king in the Escorial could not finish his paperwork.
